Kitchener Urban Tree Canopy & Park Access Analysis

A GIS analysis of tree canopy cover and park access across Kitchener's 10 wards, built entirely with open data and open-source tools. By Dennis Kurian, GIS Application Specialist.

26.5%citywide tree canopy cover
92.3%of the city within 800 m of a park
99,493public trees in the city inventory
541parks analysed
274.4 kmof trails

Key findings

  • Canopy is uneven. Ward canopy ranges from 17.2% to 34.2% against a citywide average of 26.5%.
  • Top planting priority: Ward 5. It combines the lowest canopy (17.2%) with the weakest park access (69.1% of its area within 800 m of a park) and the fewest inventoried trees per resident (277.4 per 1,000).
  • Park access is strong in the built-up wards - most sit at 95-100% within an 800 m walk of a park - so canopy, not parkland, is the main equity gap inside the urban area.
  • One species dominates. Most common inventoried trees: Norway Maple (12,774), Littleleaf Linden (5,903), Ivory Silk (4,640), Sugar Maple (4,599), Norway Maple Red Variety (4,248).

How it was done

  • Data: City of Kitchener open data (ArcGIS REST services) - municipal boundary, wards, parks, trails, the 99,493-tree public inventory, and tree cover by census dissemination area.
  • Canopy by ward: dissemination-area tree cover was apportioned to wards by areal interpolation (each area contributes cover in proportion to the land it shares with the ward).
  • Park access: parks were buffered by 800 m (about a 10-minute walk), dissolved into one service area, and intersected with each ward.
  • Tree counts: spatial join of the tree inventory points to wards, reported per 1,000 residents.
  • Planting priority score: a simple weighted overlay - (1 - canopy %) + (1 - park access %) - in the same spirit as a suitability model. Higher score = greater need.
  • Tools: Python (GeoPandas, Shapely) for the full analysis workflow; Leaflet for this web map. No proprietary GIS software was used, so the workflow is fully reproducible.

Data notes and limitations

  • Canopy vintage: canopy figures derive from the city's 2019 canopy layer, the latest the city publishes. Trees planted or removed since then are not reflected.
  • Ward canopy is an estimate: census dissemination areas do not align with ward boundaries, so tree cover was apportioned by land share (areal interpolation). This assumes canopy is spread evenly within each census area; individual ward values could differ by a point or two from a direct canopy overlay.
  • Population is interpolated: the wards layer's own population field was not usable, so ward population was interpolated from census dissemination areas the same way. Trees per 1,000 residents is therefore an estimate as well. Interpolated ward populations sum to about 256,000, consistent with the city's census population.
  • Park access is straight-line distance: the 800 m service areas are Euclidean buffers, not walking routes along the street network. True walking access would be somewhat lower. A network-based service area analysis is the natural next step.
  • Tree counts cover inventoried public trees only: the city tree inventory does not include trees on private property, although those trees do contribute to the canopy figures.
  • Parks are broadly defined: the 541 parks are all park and open-space polygons the city publishes, including natural areas.
Project by Dennis Kurian - GIS Application Specialist (Fleming College), Kitchener, Ontario. Data: City of Kitchener Open Data. Canopy figures derive from the city's 2019 canopy / tree-equity layers. This is an independent sample project, not an official City of Kitchener product.
